paper_title: The Life Cycle of a Massive Activation: Stochastic Birth, Weight-Decay-Driven Growth, and Competitive Consolidation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Massive activations, residual-stream coordinates with magnitudes far larger than typical activations, are associated with attention sinks in transformers, but how their scale is regulated during training remains incompletely understood. Combining training-trajectory analyses and controlled interventions, we trace their emergence, growth, and consolidation. Sink-carrying channels vary across random seeds but stabilize early within each run. Over longer training, surrounding channels erode and the sink concentrates onto a few redundant carriers. Across ablations, gradient attenuation follows the sink token's collective root-mean-square magnitude rather than any single channel, making collective scale central to understanding their effects. Our central result is that weight decay causally controls the turnover of global activation scale. In controlled continuations, removing decay near the peak allows this scale to keep rising, whereas retaining it produces decline even at constant learning rate. We develop a balance model for the rise and peak of massive-activation magnitude, in which AdamW-preconditioned growth opposes weight decay. Sweeping the decay coefficient $λ$ shifts peak timing approximately log-linearly and yields peak magnitudes scaling approximately as $λ^{-1/2}$, consistent with this balance. Optimizer measurements further show that preconditioning sustains the large-channel cohort against decay even when raw maintaining forces are too small to do so. Together, these findings connect the observed life cycle to scale-regulating training dynamics and establish weight decay as a training-time lever on activation magnitude.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Massive activations, residual-stream coordinates with magnitudes far larger than typical activations, are associated with attention sinks in transformers, but how their scale is regulated during training remains incompletely understood. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: A trained transformers hidden states are not uniform. In every model examined so far, handful of coordinates carry magnitudes hundreds or thousands of times the typical activation, concentrated at single token position and largely unchanging across inputs Sun et al. (2024). These massive activations are not incidental: they act as implicit attention biases (Xiao et al., 2024), model quality can degrade when they are removed (Yu et al., 2025), and they are the principal obstacle to lowprecision training and inference (Dettmers et al., 2022; Bondarenko et al., 2023; He et al., 2024). That obstacle is not fixed cost of scale: Ahmadian et al. Ahmadian et al. (2023) report that outlier dimensions are sensitive to the optimization conditions under which model is pre-trained rather than an inherent product of its size. Park et al. Park et al. (2025) take that finding as design target, replacing Adam with an optimizer chosen to avoid privileged bases and training 1.4B model on 1T tokens without the usual activation outliers. Prior work gives partial account of behaviors of these large outlier activations. Chen et al. (2026) supply mechanism for why large magnitude is useful it attenuates the gradient that accumu1 lates at an attention sink in the form of lower bound the magnitude must clear. Gallego-Feliciano et al. (2025) show that the emergence of massive activations over training is highly regular, fitting five-parameter law to their growth. These are complementary but incomplete: one is constraint and the other curve. Neither says what sets the magnitude in practice, what stops it growing, or why one coordinate rather than another comes to carry it. We address those questions, and the answer to the last turns out to govern how the first two should be read.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Massive activations and attention sinks. Sun et al. (2024) characterised massive activations as small number of near-constant, extreme-magnitude coordinates appearing at fixed feature dimensions and predominantly at the first token or at delimiters. They function as implicit attention biases: supplying the architecture with explicit learnable bias parameters removes the need for them, and they do not form. The forward-side counterpart is the attention sink (Xiao et al., 2024) disproportionate attention mass routed to an uninformative early token which Xiao et al. (2024) exploit for streaming inference by retaining sink tokens in the KV cache. Why model should want sink has since received second answer: Barbero et al. Barbero et al. (2025) argue that attending to the first token limits over-mixing of representations across depth, so the sink guards against representational collapse in long contexts. Darcet et al. (2023) report the same phenomenon in vision parallel, static line of work documents outlier dimensions as an obstacle to quantization Dettmers et al. (2022); Kovaleva et al. (2021); Bondarenko et al. (2023). further line asks why the residual stream should have privileged basis at all, given that the architecture is close to rotation-symmetric: Elhage et al. Elhage et al. (2023) rule out LayerNorm and finite-precision arithmetic as the cause and attribute the alignment to the per-dimension normalizers in Adam. That places the optimizer rather than the architecture at the origin of coordinate-aligned outliers, reading our 9 and 11 support from the training-dynamics side. The gradient-sink account. Chen et al. (2026) give the mechanistic account this paper builds on. Under causal masking, token attended to by many later positions also aggregates their gradients gradient sink. Because the normalisation Jacobian attenuates gradients in proportion to 1/rms(x), large residual magnitude at that position suppresses the accumulated gradient. Their Theorem gives sufficient condition, rms(x) γ τ gy = xL τ, (1) for any target gradient scale τ , where γ is the normalisation gain vector, gy the gradient arriving at the normalisation output, and the training loss. They test the implication with V-scale, modification attenuating gradient flow on the value path, and report that massive activations are suppressed while attention sinks persist. Two features of Equation (5) shape what follows. It is stated on rms(x), property of the whole token rather than of any coordinate. And it is one-sided: it establishes floor and penalises nothing above it, so it predicts neither peak nor decline during the training cycle and training dynamics. Emergence over training. Gallego-Feliciano et al. (2025) characterised the developmental side, fitting the max-to-median ratio across 188 layers of the Pythia suite with (t) = eλfitxt log(xt) + K, xt = γt + t0, (2) at mean R2 of 0.984, and predicting its parameters from architectural features. The law has critical point at which the ratio turns over, but the mechanism producing it was left open. On the forward side, Gu et l. Gu et al. (2025) study when the attention sink appears over pre-training and how optimization, data distribution, loss and architecture bear on whether it appears at all, reading the sink as key bias that absorbs surplus attention without contributing to the value computation. Their subject is the sinks appearance; ours is the trajectory of the massive activation that carries it, including what happens after the sink is established

sections.title: 3 BACKGROUND
sections.content: We study the life cycle of massive activations by combining measurements across training with controlled perturbations. Our approach pairs densely checkpointed training runs with analyses of released Pythia checkpoints. The experiments used to measure these quantities are setup according to details in Appendix E. Theory needed to understand these experiments is covered below.

sections.title: 3.1 ARCHITECTURE AND HIDDEN STATES
sections.content: We consider decoder-only transformers of pre-norm residual blocks. Block ℓ receives hidden state hℓ1 RSd, where is the sequence length and the model width, and returns hℓ = hℓ1 + Fℓ(Norm(hℓ1)) , (3) where Fℓ comprises multi-head self-attention and an MLP, and Norm is LayerNorm (Ba et al., 2016) or, in the variant of 3, RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019). We write hℓ for the post-residual state the residual stream and index its entries as hℓ(s, c) for token position and channel c. An activation is one such scalar. We do not examine intermediate quantities inside Fℓ except where stated. Two consequences of the pre-norm placement matter throughout. Intermediate layers see normalised inputs, so the forward computation depends on the direction of hℓ at position far more than on its scale: coordinate can grow very large without much altering what the next block computes. The backward pass is different. The Jacobian of the normalisation carries factor of order 1/rms, and that factor is not normalised away. Residual magnitude is therefore close to free in the forward direction and consequential in the backward one the asymmetry that makes large activations useful rather than merely tolerable. 3.2 THE SINK TOKEN Attention weights at each head are softmax over positions and therefore sum to one. When no position is worth attending to, the mass must still be assigned somewhere, and it accumulates at token carrying little content typically the first, which under causal masking is the only position visible to every later one, though delimiters also serve. We write for the sink position and measure all quantities there unless otherwise noted. We identify per model as the position carrying the largest activations rather than assuming position 0, since as we show it is not always position 0 (4.5). 3.3 THREE MAGNITUDES Let = hℓ(s, ) Rd be the sink tokens hidden state at layer ℓ and training step t. We use three quantities. Channel magnitude. mℓ,t(c) = xc, the value of single coordinate. This is what the perturbation experiments manipulate and what the competition among channels is fought over. Ratio. Following Gallego-Feliciano et al. (2025), rℓ,t = maxc xc mediancxc , (4) the max-to-median ratio, to which Equation (8) was fitted. We retain it for comparability with that work. Root-mean-square. in Equation (5). It is property of the token, not of any channel. rmsℓ,t = x2, the tokens aggregate scale, and the quantity appearing (cid:113) 1 These three do not move together, and conflating them is the easiest way to misread the phenomenon. In particular has denominator that is itself changing: over training the median falls, so can rise while the numerator of the dominant channel is falling. We observe exactly this (4.1).

sections.title: 3.4 WHAT COUNTS AS A MASSIVE ACTIVATION
sections.content: Sun et al. (2024) define an activation as massive when > 100 and a/median(hℓ) 1000. As noted in Gallego-Feliciano et al. (2025), these absolute thresholds do not transfer to smaller models, which exhibit the same qualitative pattern at lower values, and we follow that work in identifying the massive activation as the largest-magnitude channel at the sink of the layer where is greatest. Under threshold definition the question is settled by fiat; using the argmax instead lets us measure whether the winner is distinct category or merely the top of continuum. We therefore also report the isolation of the leading channels: the largest ratio between consecutive entries of the sorted sink-magnitude profile. Isolation near 1 indicates populated continuum; large isolation indicates small set standing apart from collapsed bulk. We use cohort for the leading channels above that gap.

sections.title: 3.5 GRADIENT QUANTITIES
sections.content: The mechanism under test concerns the backward pass, so we measure gradients as well as activations. We write gx for the gradient with respect to the sink tokens representation at the input to blocks normalisation. Chen et al. (2026) show that, under RMSNorm, this gradient is attenuated by the tokens own scale, gx γ gy rms(x) , (5) where γ is the normalisation gain and gy the gradient at the normalisation output. LayerNorms Jacobian carries the same 1/rms(x) factor up to centring, so the prediction applies to both variants. Equation (5) is the relation our ablations test in 4.3. channel is written into the residual stream by particular rows of the output-projection matrices of the blocks below it. We call these the channels writer rows and collect them as w. channels magnitude grows or shrinks according to whether the loss-driven force on exceeds the pull of weight decay, which we quantify by the maintaining force = w, gw w2 , (6) where gw is the gradient on the writer rows and , denotes the Frobenius inner product. The numerator measures how strongly the loss pushes along its own direction; normalising by w2 makes fractional growth rate, directly comparable to the weight-decay coefficient λ, which enters the AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) update as η(gw + λw). The channel therefore grows when > λ and erodes otherwise. Two versions of Equation (6) appear below and they differ substantially. The raw maintaining force uses gw directly. The preconditioned force applies AdamWs second-moment normalisation gw (Kingma & Ba, 2015), dividing each element by the square root of its accumulated squared gradient. Because small but persistent gradient has correspondingly small second moment, preconditioning can amplify it by orders of magnitude. As we show (4.7), the raw force on every large channel falls far below λ so the sink cannot be sustained by raw gradient magnitude at all while the preconditioned force does not. Statements about what maintains channel must therefore be made after preconditioning; instantaneous raw gradients do not read these dynamics.

sections.title: 4 RESULTS
sections.content: We examine how massive activations develop, how their magnitude is regulated, and how they concentrate onto small cohort. We first characterise activation trajectories and the role of weight decay in global turnover. We then use ablations and magnitude-matched controls to distinguish effects of channel identity from effects of magnitude and collective scale. Finally, we examine stochastic channel identity, scale, and training maturity, distinguishing optimiser-mediated cohort maintenance from the unresolved mechanism of survivor selection. 4 Figure 1: Weight decay causes the turnover. (a) Global scale (median x) rises without weight decay and declines with it, including at constant learning rate. The decaying schedule amplifies the decline. (b) MA peak location varies approximately log-linearly with the decay coefficient (corr = 0.985). 4.1 MASSIVE ACTIVATIONS EMERGE AND FOLLOW GLOBAL LAW The dominant-layer max/median ratio follows the previously reported five-parameter law (GallegoFeliciano et al., 2025), while sizeable channels share rise-and-decline pattern in raw magnitude. These quantities need not move together: the ratio can continue rising while the MA magnitude falls because the median decreases faster. Full trajectories, fit results, and the qualifications on the peak-location analysis are provided in Appendices and C. 4.2 WEIGHT DECAY CAUSES THE TURNOVER Continuing from near-peak checkpoint without weight decay, the global activation scale (median x) keeps rising. With weight decay, it falls even at constant learning rate: 11% over the compared window, versus 18% under the decaying schedule (Fig. 1a). Thus, in these continuations, weight decay drives the global turnover and the schedule amplifies the decline. This causal comparison concerns the global median: the individual MA is noisier and plateaus rather than declines at constant learning rate. Sweeping the decay coefficient under the schedule shifts the MAs peak location approximately log-linearly, tpeak ln λ (corr = 0.985; Fig. 1b). At λ = 0, no peak occurs within the observation window. Peak magnitude scales approximately as λ1/2, consistent with the rise-andpeak balance model in A. 4.3 THE GRADIENT FLOOR IS ON THE TOKENS COLLECTIVE RMS The gradient-sink bound predicts gx 1/rms(x) (Equation (5)). We ablate the MA and other large channels individually, measuring (rms(x), gx) with one forward and backward pass per condition and no training. The product gxrms(x) remains approximately constant across ablation conditions: 0.94 when the MA is ablated, within the 0.890.95 range spanned by ablations of the other large channels (Fig. 2a). Ablating the MA changes the tokens rms by only approximately 5%. These measurements support attenuation governed by the tokens collective rms, with the MA one of several contributors rather than an exceptional channel. 4.4 APPARENT MA-SPECIFIC REGULATION RESOLVES TO MAGNITUDE In perturb-and-restore experiments, an ablated MA is rebuilt (a floor), while an over-driven MA is pulled back during decline (a ceiling). These responses exceed those of matched-norm random channel and occur independently of weight decay, initially suggesting MA-specific regulation. However, the random channel differs in activation magnitude, motivating magnitude-matched controls. 5 Figure 2: Controls: apparent MA-specificity resolves to magnitude. (a) Across individualchannel ablations, the downstream sink gradient follows gx 1/rms(x); the MA lies with the other large channels. (b) Matched-rms displacements show similar pullback despite different direction distortions, supporting collective-scale interpretation of the declining-regime ceiling. Pythia-410m has no pairwise top-three overlap across the three seeds; the two 51M runs share one secondary channel. The ceiling tracks collective rms. We compare scaling the MA alone with scaling the top-16 channels proportionally, matched for the induced rms displacement. Despite an 11 difference in direction distortion, the two perturbations remove similar fractions of the rms excess: 73% and 71%, respectively (Fig. 2b). small random channel shows only approximately 20% pullback. The measured ceiling therefore tracks aggregate magnitude rather than uniquely responding to the MA or its direction distortion. These comparisons concern the continuum regime of the 51M model; 4.6 examines when comparable-magnitude peers exist. Gain suppression is also large-channel effect. The MAs LayerNorm gain is comparable to that of other large channels rather than uniquely suppressed (Appendix D, Fig. 9). 4.5 THE MASSIVE ACTIVATION IS STOCHASTIC ROLE, NOT FIXED DIMENSION Changing the training seed while holding architecture and data fixed changes the sink-carrying coordinates. In our 51M model, the dominant channel is 207 under one seed and 263 under another; three seeds of Pythia-410m share no top-three sink channels  (Table 1)  . The number of sink channels (one to three), birth layer, and sink position also vary across seeds. Channel identity is therefore stochastic outcome of training rather than fixed architectural coordinate. The identity stabilises early  (Fig. 3)  . In Pythia-410m, the eventual top three occupy ranks 13 from approximately step 4k through the end of the 143k-step run. Ranks at 8k already correlate with final ranks (Spearman 0.50.7), while channel remaining at rank 4 later collapses in magnitude. In our 51M model, the argmax migrates from channel 221 to 308 to 207, then locks by approximately step 5k. The top-three identity also remains unchanged across ten unrelated text passages. Together, these observations support early stochastic symmetry-breaking followed by stable, input-robust sink identity. 6 Figure 3: Early lock-in of sink channels. Magnitude rank versus training step (rank 1 is largest; log axes). (a) Pythia-410ms winners settle at ranks 13 by approximately 4k steps; the rank-4 channel later collapses  (Fig. 10)  . (b) The 51M models argmax migrates 221 308 207 before locking by approximately 5k steps. Figure 4: Scale, training maturity, and isolation. (a) Separation (max /median) versus parameter count. Our models fall within Pythias range but are trained much less. (b) Isolation, the largest consecutive-rank magnitude ratio (3), across Pythia training. The shaded band shows our models over their 1040k-step horizons. (c) Separation and isolation normalised by their final values in Pythia-410m: separation settles earlier, while isolation continues growing. 4.6 SCALE AND TRAINING MATURITY SET WHETHER THE MA STANDS APART Magnitude-matched controls require channels comparable to the MA. We examine this condition using ranked sink-channel magnitudes in our from-scratch models and Pythia (70M6.9B; Fig. 4). Separation from the typical channel (max /median) increases with scale in both families, and our models fall within Pythias range. However, the from-scratch models are trained much less, so this comparison mixes scale with training maturity. Their magnitude profiles remain populated continua, whereas fully trained Pythia models have few large channels separated from collapsed bulk. Isolation also develops during training at fixed model size. Pythia-410m and 1.4B begin near isolation 1, with Pythia-410m reaching approximately 17 by 143k steps (Fig. 4b). Our models remain in the low-isolation regime over their 1040k-step training horizons, where magnitude-matched controls are available; those comparisons do not establish the same conclusions in the separated regime. Separation and isolation evolve differently. In Pythia-410m, separation largely settles by approximately 104 steps, while isolation continues increasing through the end of training (Fig. 4c). Magnitude growth and the emergence of gap between the leading cohort and the bulk are distinct processes. 7 Figure 5: AdamW preconditioning sustains the sink cohort. The preconditioned maintaining force of Equation (6), over three checkpoints. The cohort of winners and collapsers lies above Pythias decay threshold λ = 0.01 (dashed), while random channels lie near zero. Raw forces are approximately 104. Winners and collapsers overlap, leaving intra-cohort selection unresolved. 4.7 BIRTH AND DEATH: COMPETITIVE CONSOLIDATION OF THE SINK Concentration without conservation. From step 16k to 143k in Pythia-410m, the surviving channels rise and then decline mildly, while mid-rank channels erode gradually on staggered schedules  (Fig. 10)  . The top-threes share of the sink tokens squared norm x2 grows from 0.55 to 0.99. This is not redistribution of conserved quantity: total sink rms peaks and declines, and winner gain is approximately 2.9 times field loss. In the 51M continuum regime, decline is graded rather than selective: peak-to-end retention ranges from 0.78 to 0.89 across the top eight channels, with the MA part of this pattern rather than separate from it. The sink is redundant collective. In Pythia-410m at step 16k, ablating single surviving channel reduces attention to the sink by only 0.0040.015, whereas ablating the top three jointly produces drop of 0.08, an approximately 3 superadditive effect. Random-channel ablations have negligible effect  (Fig. 11)  . This supports redundant implementation of the sink, consistent with the collective-rms result (4.3) and attention-sink accounts (Sun et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2024). AdamW preconditioning sustains the cohort. Raw maintaining forces are of order 104, below Pythias λ = 102 decay coefficient in the optimiser-force comparison. After AdamW secondmoment normalization, the large-channel cohort lies above the decay threshold, while random channels remain near zero  (Fig. 5)  . Thus the measured cohort maintenance depends on optimiser preconditioning rather than raw gradient magnitude. This does not identify mechanism selecting survivors: winners and collapsers overlap in preconditioned maintaining force. Tested mechanisms and unresolved selection. The measurements do not support several candidate explanations. Collapsing channels writer-row gradients do not fall as 1/rms: the product of writer-row gradient norm and rms rises 1.52, and their gradients remain comparable to those of survivors. Across seed re-runs at 70M and 160M, survivor count does not track total sink attention (correlation 0), providing no support for count set by attention-sink saturation. Total sink rms is not conserved, as shown above, and matched-rms perturbations do not support an MA-specific ceiling (4.4). Early identity lock-in (4.5) and cohort-level maintenance do not explain why some cohort members survive and others collapse. survivor can even exhibit negative maintaining force on held-out text. These post-hoc gradient measurements do not identify an intra-cohort selector; that mechanism remains unresolved.

sections.title: 5 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
sections.content: Together, our results describe life cycle of stochastic birth, decay-controlled turnover, and competitive consolidation. Sink-carrying channels vary across seeds but stabilise early within each run; continued training erodes the surrounding field and concentrates the sink onto small, redundant cohort. Weight decay causally drives turnover in global activation scale, while the massive activations rise and peak are consistent with balance between optimiser-preconditioned growth and decay (Appendix A). Its subsequent decline reflects reduced activation per unit writer-weight norm, not necessarily shrinking weights. AdamWs second-moment normalisation sustains the cohort against decay, but the measured maintaining force does not distinguish eventual survivors. The central distinction is between channel identity and collective magnitude. Across the tested ablations, gradient attenuation follows gx 1/rms(x), locating the effect in the sink tokens aggregate scale rather than any single coordinate. In the continuum regime, magnitude-matched controls resolve apparent MA-specific regulation into magnitude effects. functional role for massive activations and magnitude-organised training dynamics are therefore compatible descriptions at different levels. These findings have consequences for how massive activations are interpreted and targeted. Because the role is stochastic filled by whichever channels win an early symmetry-breaking competition interventions that zero or suppress individual channels may leave the underlying role intact: the sink will reconstitute on different coordinates, as the seed experiments confirm. Because gradient attenuation is governed by the sink tokens collective RMS rather than any privileged dimension, the effect is distributed across the cohort and not uniquely attributable to the largest channel. Mitigation strategies that target the tokens aggregate scale, rather than individual outliers, are therefore better motivated by the present account. These conclusions are limited by experimental scale and training regime. Identity and life-cycle analyses include Pythia models spanning 70M-6.9B parameters, whereas perturb-and-restore controls remain at approximately 51M. Magnitude-matched comparisons require populated tail and do not establish the same behavior in the bimodal, late-training regime. We do not test the attention-bias function (Sun et al., 2024) or rebuilding when denied home (Vemula, 2026); intra-cohort survivor selection also remains unresolved. Within this scope, massive activation is not privileged architectural coordinate, but training-selected contributor to collective sink. (a) The MA writer norm grows linearly in prepeak (not exponentially), then bends over as the balance = λw is reached (λ = 0.1). (b) The peak MA magnitude scales as λ1/2 across weight-decay sweep (measured slope 0.51), fixing the drive exponent = 1. THEORY: BALANCE CONDITION, AND WHERE THE DECLINE LIVES Let be the aggregate writer weights feeding the MA channel; to leading order the MA magnitude w. Under AdamW, wt+1 = wt η(gw + λwt), where gw ˆµt/( ˆνt + ϵ) is the preconditioned update not the raw gradient, from which it differs by one to two orders of magnitude on these weights (4.7). Squaring and discarding the O(η2) term gives dt w2 2η(w, gw + λw2), so grows while the updates projection onto opposes decay, and turns over when the preconditioned maintaining force of Equation (6) falls to the decay coefficient: G(t) = λ. (7) This is the growth criterion of 3 evaluated at the peak, with the preconditioned drive balancing the decay pull, an equality complementing (Chen et al., 2026). This is the single-channel form of general property of training under decoupled weight decay. Kosson et al. (2024) show that AdamW drives weight vectors towards rotational equilibrium in which the expected growth contributed by the update balances the shrinkage contributed by decay, so the equilibrium scale is set by λ and the drive rather than by the loss alone. Their analysis concerns units made scale-invariant by following normalisation, whereas our are writer rows into the residual stream and are only partially scaleinvariant under pre-norm; we therefore take (7) as calibrated by the λ-sweep of 4.2 rather than inherited from that result. What the connection supplies is the expectation that balance exists at all. Assuming the un-normalised preconditioned drive G = ˆw, gw, with ˆw = w/w, follows power law in magnitude, G = mq, substituting into Equation (7) with gives mq1 λ, hence mpeak λ1/(1q) for = 1. The measured peak-magnitude scaling ( λ1/2; slope 0.51 to 0.57 across estimators, Fig. 6b) fixes = 1: the drive falls as 1/m, so each further increment of magnitude is worth progressively less. Because is defined on the preconditioned update, this characterises the optimisers effective drive rather than the loss landscape directly; the two need not share an exponent, and we do not assume they do. Directly measured, pre-peak (not exponentially), the balance = λw holds at the peak, and grows as falls over training (Fig. 6a). The decline is not weight shrinkage. At baseline weight decay the MA magnitude turns over while its writer weights keep growing: at λ = 0.1, rises 10.8 11.5 across the activations decline while the ratio m/w falls 4.2 3.2. Only at strong decay does itself contract. The same weights therefore produce less activation than before, and the decline is change in that relationship rather than in the weights size. We do not claim that weight decay shrinks the MA weights. What causes the ratio to fall we do not establish. Scope of the balance law. Equation (7) rests on and describes the rise and peak, where it is calibrated via the λ-sweep. It does not govern the decline, precisely because that proportionality breaks there. Two consequences follow. The fractional-decline prediction of the single-channel G(m) = mq does not carry over to the declining, multi-channel population: the cross-channel retention ordering during the decline (larger channels retained more; 4.7) is competition phenomenon of that regime, not consequence of this equation. And = 1 is fixed by the MAs own peak scaling rather than being universal cross-channel law. The balance condition and the competitive consolidation are accounts of two stages of the life cycle, and we do not conflate them. Honest negatives, and their positive form. We could not read the regulation off instantaneous raw gradients (activationor weight-space, multi-batch averaged); the signal is below chance and entangled with Adam preconditioning. 4.7 turns this into quantitative statement: the raw maintaining gradient is one-to-two orders below the weight-decay pull at every large channel, so the sink is held up not by raw gradient magnitude but by AdamWs second-moment normalizationthe regulation is an emergent optimiser-preconditioning effect, visible under displacement or after preconditioning but not in the raw gradient. direction test did not isolate representational cost for the ceiling. EMERGENCE-LAW FIT The max/median ratio of the dominant layer follows the five-parameter emergence law of GallegoFeliciano et al. (2025), r(t) = eκxt log xt + K, xt = τ + t0, (8) with amplitude A, decay rate κ, time scaling τ , time offset t0 and asymptotic baseline K. We rename the last two from the λ, γ of Gallego-Feliciano et al., which here denote weight decay and the normalisation gain. The fit attains R2 = 0.999 over 40k steps in the 51M model  (Fig. 7)  . The ratio and the raw magnitude can disagree in direction: at layer 5, the ratio rises monotonically to approximately 400, while the underlying MA magnitude peaks near step 20k and then declines, because the median falls faster than the MA. The ratio therefore reflects changes in both the dominant channels magnitude and the median, rather than the dominant channels magnitude alone. Figure 7: MAs emerge and fit the five-parameter law of (Gallego-Feliciano et al., 2025) (R2 = 0.999; layer 5, 51M model). GLOBAL CHANNEL-MAGNITUDE DYNAMICS Measuring per-channel magnitudes directly (Fig. 8a, layer 2), essentially every sizeable channel rises and then declines: 98/98 at layer 2 and 382/398 at layer 5. The peak location tends to increase with amplitude (Fig. 8b), with small channels peaking early and large channels peaking late, and the MA at the extreme. This relationship is noisy and right-censored. Channels whose peaks occur beyond the 40k-step observation window cannot appear in the peak-location analysis, biasing its high-amplitude end downward. We therefore interpret the relationship as tendency rather than clean law. The riseand-decline shape is shared across the sizeable-channel population rather than being specific to the MA; the five-parameter ratio law reflects both this magnitude dynamic and the falling median. Figure 8: The rise-and-decline is global. (a) Per-channel sink magnitude (layer 2): nearly all sizeable channels rise then decline; the MA is the large-amplitude tail. (b) Peak location vs. channel peak magnitude, pooled over layers; the binned median (line) rises with amplitude, but the perchannel scatter is wide at any amplitude and right-censoredchannels peaking beyond the 40k-step window cannot appear, biasing the high-amplitude end downwardso we read tendency, not clean law.

sections.title: D LAYERNORM GAIN SUPPRESSION
sections.content: On the unperturbed trajectory, the massive activations magnitude rises and persists while its normalisation gain γ falls from approximately 1.0 early in training to 0.69 by the end of training (Fig. 9a). The suppression is not peculiar to the massive activation. At the layer where it is largest, gain decreases with magnitude across the whole population, and every one of the top eight channels sits at γ 0.650.84, against bulk median of approximately 1.25. The massive activation, at γ = 0.69, lies among its equal-magnitude peers rather than below them (Fig. 9b). As with the floor and the ceiling, what looks like an MA-specific property is property of being large.

sections.title: E EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: E.1 MODELS AND TRAINING We train decoder-only transformers from scratch at three scales, which we label by their parameter counts: 51M (8 layers, width 512, 8 heads), 203M (12 layers, width 1024, 16 heads), and 380M (16 layers, width 1280, 16 heads). All use context length 512, the GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) bytepair vocabulary (50,304 tokens), no bias terms, learned positional embeddings, and tied input/output embeddings, and are trained on the Dolma corpus (Soldaini et al., 2024). The primary model uses LayerNorm, with an RMSNorm variant at matched configuration for architecture-generality. Optimization uses AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) (β = (0.9, 0.95), gradient clipping at 1.0) with weight decay λ = 0.1 and peak learning rate of 6 104 decayed by cosine schedule to 6 105 after linear warmup of 300 steps (400 for the two larger models). The effective batch is 96 sequences of length 512 for the 51M model (64 and 40 for the 203M and 380M models), in bfloat16. The three models train for 40k, 20k, and 10k steps, corresponding to approximately 14 Figure 9: Gain suppression tracks magnitude, not identity. (a) Over training the massive activations magnitude rises and holds while its LayerNorm gain γ falls from approximately 1.0 to 0.69. (b) At the layer where the massive activation is largest, γ decreases with channel magnitude across the population; the top eight channels all sit far below the bulk median, and the massive activation lies among them. 2.0B, 0.7B, and 0.2B tokens. Runs use seeds 1337 (primary) and 2024 (second seed). Checkpoints including optimiser state are saved every 500 steps and activation probes recorded every 50 steps. For the identity, scale, and consolidation analyses we additionally use released Pythia checkpoints (Biderman et al., 2023) at 70M, 160M, 410M, 1.4B, 2.8B, and 6.9B parameters, including the seed re-runs at 70M, 160M, and 410M, and the 150 intermediate training checkpoints released per model. These are analysed by inference only; no Pythia model is trained or fine-tuned here. E.2 PROBES Activations are measured at the sink position of each layer over fixed batch of 24 sequences of length 512 from the validation split, held constant across checkpoints so that trajectories are comparable (for Pythia, fixed passage of held-out text). At each probe we record the per-layer ratio r, the rms of the sink token, the full ranked profile of channel magnitudes not only the argmax, so that near-degeneracy between the leading channels is visible the identity of the argmax channel and its layer, and the norms of the writer rows for the leading channels. E.3 PERTURBATION PROTOCOL To ask whether channel is actively maintained rather than passively accumulated, we displace it and observe what training does. From checkpoint we create forks sharing batch order and learning rate frozen at its value at the fork. In each fork the target channels writer rows are scaled by factor α at every layer single-layer intervention is insufficient, since the channel is written redundantly across depth (4.7). We use α = 1 as an unperturbed control, which establishes how far two runs drift from data ordering alone; α = 0 to test for restoring force from below; and α = 2 to test for one from above. Forks resume for 200300 steps, with replicate resume seeds where error bars are reported. We report the perturbed forks absolute trajectory alongside its gap to the control. This matters because the control is itself moving during both the rising and declining phases, so closing gap does not by itself demonstrate that anything is being restored. Recovery is summarised by the fraction of the initial gap closed within the window and by the half-recovery time, which is more robust than an exponential time constant when the return is not single-exponential. E.4 CONTROLLING FOR MAGNITUDE The perturbation protocol answers whether channel responds; it does not answer whether the response is peculiar to that channel. randomly chosen channel differs from the massive activation in magnitude, so comparing the two confounds identity with size. Since almost every quantity we measure varies with magnitude, that confound is not incidental. We therefore compare against equal magnitude wherever the comparison is available, by three means. First, we regress the property of interest on channel magnitude and ask whether the massive activation lies above the value its own magnitude predicts. The trend must be fitted on channels well below the massive activation and the leading channels scored against it out-of-sample; trend fitted on all remaining channels is contaminated by the runners-up, which are close in magnitude and can depress the high end enough to manufacture an apparent outlier where none exists (4.4). Second, we match perturbations for the change they induce in rms: single-channel displacement and one distributed proportionally across the leading channels are scaled to produce the same increase in the tokens aggregate magnitude, so that the comparison isolates what distinguishes them how far each rotates the tokens direction rather than how far each moved rms. Third, we pool across layers, architectures, and seeds, and require at least 10 channels per group before reporting any differentiator, having twice found clean separations at smaller samples dissolve under proper sampling. This control has precondition, examined in 4.6: there must exist channels of comparable magnitude to serve as the reference. Whether they do is property of the training regime rather than fixed fact about transformers. Weight-decay causal test (4.2). Starting from near-peak checkpoint of the 51 model, we resume training under two conditions sharing an identical batch order: weight decay enabled at the checkpoints λ, and weight decay disabled (λ = 0). The optimizers accumulated first and second moments are carried over from the checkpoint; only the weight decay field of each parameter group is overridden. Both runs continue for 8,000 steps with gradient accumulation over four microbatches of 24 sequences, and activations are probed every 100 steps on the fixed validation batch. To isolate the effect of weight decay from that of the cosine learning-rate schedule, one variant holds the learning rate fixed at the checkpoint value; the comparison in 4.2 uses this constant rate fork. second variant follows the schedule, which amplifies the decline but is not required for the qualitative result. The dose-response curve (Fig. 1b) is obtained by re-running the same protocol at λ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4} under the cosine schedule and recording the training step at which the MA channel reaches its maximum magnitude in each run. Peak locations are fit to tpeak ln λ by ordinary least squares. Gradient floor test (4.3). We test whether the product gx rms(x) is constant across ablation conditions, as predicted by Eq. 5, or whether ablating the MA channel produces an outlier. Layer and channel selection. The target layer is the layer with the highest max/median ratio, identified automatically via the activation probe on the fixed validation batch. The MA channel is the coordinate of highest mean absolute activation at position over the probe batch; six comparison channels are taken as the next-highest by the same criterion, excluding the MA. Ablation. Each channel is ablated by zeroing its writer rows across all layers (α = 0 in the notation of E.3), using fresh copy of the checkpoint loaded for each condition. Gradient extraction. To obtain gx = L/hL at the sink position, we register forward hook on block and call retain grad() on its output tensor, which PyTorch would otherwise discard as non-leaf intermediate. The model is set to training mode to enable gradient tracking, but no optimizer step is taken. single forward and backward pass through the cross-entropy loss is run on the fixed probe batch of 24 sequences. We extract the residual-stream vector = hL[s, :] and its gradient = L/hL[s, :] at sink position s, then average rms(x) = x2 and over the batch. (cid:113) 16 Test statistic. For each ablation condition we report gi rmsi (constant under the pure 1/rms law) and the ratio gi / (g0 rms0/rmsi), where subscript 0 denotes the unablated control. ratio near 1.0 across all conditions indicates that attenuation is governed by the collective token scale rather than the identity of any individual channel. Apparent MA-specific regulation (4.4). Section 4.4 reports two classes of perturbation: floor experiment (ablated MA is rebuilt by continued training) and ceiling experiment (over-driven MA relaxes back), followed by direction-controlled comparison that resolves the apparent specificity to magnitude effect. Floor and ceiling (perturb-and-restore). Following the protocol of E.3, we create three forks from each checkpoint: an unperturbed control (α = 1), perturbed MA fork (α = 0 for the floor; α = 2 for the ceiling), and fork perturbing random channel matched by writer-row L2 norm to the MA. All forks share batch order and resume with the learning rate frozen at its checkpoint value. Forks run for 200300 steps and recovery is summarised by the fraction of the initial perturbation gap closed within the window and the model-free half-recovery time t1/2. Ceiling with matched-norm random channel. For the ceiling comparison, the random channel is selected as the channel whose aggregate writer-row L2 norm is closest to the MAs, excluding the MA itself. Both the MA and the random channel are scaled by α = 2 in separate forks. Recovery is measured as the fraction of the initial excess magnitude (m0 m0/α) removed by the end of the window: (m0 mend)/(m0 m0/α). Direction-controlled comparison (Fig. 2b). To test whether the ceiling reflects MA identity or aggregate token scale, we compare two perturbations from the same checkpoint that induce equal rms displacement at the sink but differ in direction distortion by factor of 11: Kick A: scale the MA channel alone by α = 2, strongly distorting the sink direction. Kick B: scale the top-16 channels by factor β, calibrated iteratively (up to three passes, convergence tolerance 3%) so that the resulting rms(x) matches Kick A, preserving the sink direction. Both forks resume for 300 steps. We track rms(xsink) and the cosine distortion 1 cos(ˆxt, ˆxctrl each step, where ˆxctrl is the unit sink vector of the unperturbed control at the same step. ) at Scale and isolation profiles (4.6). Section 4.6 reports two measurements: cross-model snapshot at the end of training (Fig. 4a), and trajectory of isolation over training in Pythia-410m (Fig. 4bc). Cross-model scale profile. For the 51 from-scratch model we use the final checkpoint (step 40k) with the fixed probe batch (E.2), hooking all layers simultaneously to obtain residual-stream activations. For Pythia models (70M6.9B) we load the final released weights from Hugging Face, pass single fixed passage of 512 tokens (batch size 4) through output hidden states, and collect all layer outputs in one forward pass. In both cases the target layer is identified automatically as the layer with the highest max/median ratio across all layers and token positions. We report two complementary measures of how far the leading channels stand apart from the rest: Separation (max / median): the ratio of the largest channel magnitude to the median across channels at the sink position, following Eq. 4. Isolation (cliff): the largest ratio between adjacent entries in the top-15 sorted magnitude profile, max13 i=0 (si/si+1), where s0 s1 are the sorted magnitudes. large cliff indicates that the leading cohort has pulled away from the remainder; cliff near 1 indicates populated continuum. trajectory (Pythia-410m). Isolation checkpoints {1k, 2k, 4k, 8k, 16k, 32k, 64k, 143k} steps, passing the same fixed passage (batch size 4, sequence length 512) at each. Separation and isolation are computed identically to the cross-model profile above, with the target layer re-identified independently at each checkpoint. Figure 4c normalises each quantity by its value at the final checkpoint to place them on common scale. Pythia-410m at load We 17 Figure 10: Competitive consolidation in Pythia-410m (16k143k steps). (a) The top-three winners rise and then decline mildly, while mid-rank channels erode on staggered schedules. (b) Isolation builds continuously rather than appearing at single transition step. Figure 11: The sink is redundant collective. Drop in sink attention after channel ablation (Pythia-410m, step 16k). Individual surviving-channel ablations have small effects; joint top-three ablation is approximately 3 superadditive. random-channel ablation has negligible effect. Competitive consolidation (4.7). Section 4.7 reports three separate measurements on Pythia410m: retention analysis of channel magnitudes over training, an attention-ablation test of redundancy, and an optimizer-state measurement of cohort maintenance. All three use the released Pythia-410m checkpoints loaded from Hugging Face. Retention and concentration  (Fig. 10)  . Starting from the checkpoint at step 16k (near the emergence onset), we track the magnitude of each channel at the sink position across checkpoints at steps {16k, 30k, 60k, 90k, 120k, 143k}. Retention for rank at step is defined as mag(t) / mag(16k), normalising each channels trajectory to its value at the reference checkpoint. We report the mean retention for the top-3 winners and for the mid-tier (ranks 412 at step 16k) separately. Redundancy test  (Fig. 11)  . To measure how much each channel contributes to the attention sink, we ablate channels by zeroing them via forward hooks registered on the embedding layer and on every transformer layer output, so that the ablated channel carries no signal at any depth. We then measure the mean attention weight assigned to position 0 from all query positions 1, averaged across all heads and all layers, on single 256-token sequence. Survivors (channels 357, 130, 966) and collapser (channel 752) are ablated individually and jointly; three randomly sampled channels serve as baseline. Superadditivity is the ratio of the joint top-three drop to the sum of the individual drops. AdamW preconditioning  (Fig. 5)  . We measure the preconditioned maintaining force = w, ˆgw / w2 (Eq. 6) for three groups of channels at steps 16k, 32k, and 48k. Channel groups are defined from the step-16k and step-143k checkpoints: winners are the top10 channels by magnitude at step 143k; collapsers are channels in the top-40 at step 16k 18 whose retention mag(143k)/mag(16k) < 0.2 and that are not winners; random channels are drawn uniformly from the remainder. At each checkpoint we accumulate per-sample gradients over 200 batches of 128 tokens from WikiText-2, computing the mean gradient and mean squared gradient per writer-row entry. The preconditioned gradient is ˆgw = / ( + ε), approximating AdamWs second-moment normalisation. Writer rows are the rows of the attention output projection (attention.dense.weight) and the MLP down-projection (mlp.dense 4h to h.weight) indexed by channel. The decay threshold λ = 0.01 is Pythias weight-decay coefficient.
